Quand on est demandeur d’asile, les diff: For asylum seekers, the difficulties don't end once they arrive in Canada. With the pandemic, these difficulties seem to have worsened, upending the hearing process. Linda* staked her future in Quebec from her living room. Originally from Cameroon, she had her asylum hearing in early November, making her one of the first to go through a virtual hearing. Her lawyer was at her own home, so Linda was alone in front of her screen.
« J’ai vu le commissaire [de la Commissi: “I saw the commissioner [from the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB)]. There were other people behind, but I never saw their faces, just their names. During the questioning, I couldn’t see my lawyer, it was just me and the commissioner. That can be intimidating for some people,” she explains. Before the pandemic, claimants were summoned with their lawyer to the offices of the imposing Guy-Favreau Complex on René-Lévesque Boulevard.
Après avoir repris en présentiel <l1>à l: After resuming in person <l1>in mid-September</l1>, with plexiglass on the tables and everyone wearing a mask, asylum hearings have been held virtually since October 2020. This digital shift can have its pitfalls. Frantz André, president of the Comité d’action des personnes sans statut, fears that asylum seekers will suffer from this imposed distance between participants.
« On déshumanise une question humanitair: “We’re dehumanizing a humanitarian issue. The commissioner can’t see the claimant sweating from stress, for example,” he says, referring to all the non-verbal cues that don’t show up within the frame of a camera. The activist says the start was difficult for technological reasons: connection or sound problems, not being able to see the participants, and so on.
Mais quelques semaines plus tard, chacun: But a few weeks later, everyone is starting to get used to the new way of doing things. Linda explains that she and her lawyer ran a mock hearing to test the computers. “It can be hard for someone who isn’t familiar with computers,” she admits, not to mention that access to technology can be difficult for some. Still, Linda strongly preferred testifying by camera.
« J’ai préféré rester à la maison. Ne pa: “I preferred staying home. Not being at immigration, between four walls with all those people, reassured me a lot,” she explains. Having to appear in person would have been far more stressful for her.
Linda et son fils sont entrés au Québec: Linda and her son entered Quebec in April 2018 through Roxham Road. As soon as she arrived, she was given a list of legal aid lawyers to help her with her asylum claim. Two years and seven months later, in October 2020, she was summoned to a hearing to take place four weeks after that. The federal government can take up to three years to review a claim and summon the person to a hearing before the IRB. This hearing can determine a person’s life. While there is the possibility of an appeal, of an application to the Federal Court and, as a last resort, of filing a humanitarian application, the chances of obtaining refuge are slim if the first decision was negative. “The acceptance rate on appeal is 5%, and it’s close to zero at the Federal Court,” says Frantz André.
Ce n’est justement pas l’audience en ell: It wasn’t the hearing itself that caused Linda the most anguish, but the uncertainty behind that endless wait.
Les délais de traitement étaient déjà lo: Processing times were already long before February 2020, but with the pandemic, hearings were postponed and <l1>many activities</l1> and procedures were slowed down, or even stopped altogether. “I got an answer right away, but I know people who had their hearing in January or February and still have no answer,” says Linda.
Une telle attente permet de rester au Qu: Such a wait allows a person to stay in Quebec, work and settle into a home, but it keeps them in a precarious status.
« J’étais stressée de ne pas encore avoi: “I was stressed about not having had my hearing yet. Especially when I saw people who arrived after me having theirs before me. You’re here, you’re building your life, but you don’t know if you can stay,” she explains.
Alors que dans bien des cas, il ne serai: Yet in many cases, it wouldn’t necessarily be necessary to go all the way to a hearing, according to Stéphanie Valois, an immigration lawyer. “Any woman from Sudan or Iran should automatically be granted asylum. Some cases are so clear-cut!” she says. Some cases are accepted outright if they meet certain criteria.
C’est le cas des demandes de personnes f: That is the case for claims from people fleeing Yemen, where war has been ravaging the country since 2016. Conversely, <l1>the board requires</l1> a hearing on a long list of sometimes subjective criteria, such as the need to look further into “questions related to the claimant’s identity.” “It would take more courage on the part of the IRB to accept more of the clear-cut cases,” says Stéphanie Valois.
Mais au-delà de ces nouveaux enjeux appo: But beyond these new issues brought on by the health crisis, there are others that have outlasted the pandemic. Notably when the lawyer or the interpreter comes from the same country as the claimant. “The lawyer who will exploit you the most is the one who is from the same background as you,” says Frantz André, who has documented serious errors in the files of the claimants he has supported. Just last July, three Hungarian lawyers in Toronto were found guilty of systemic negligence in the files of Roma asylum seekers from Hungary. The <l1>class action</l1> resulted in $500,000 CAD in compensation.
Même chose du côté des interprètes. Afin: The same goes for interpreters. To ensure clear communication, every asylum seeker can be accompanied by an interpreter. However, with certain dialects and languages, the interpreter is likely to come from the same place as the claimant. “Knowing this, the person fears there will be leaks or value judgments. For example, in cases of sexual violence, there will be an enormous barrier to talking about it in front of the interpreter,” explains Chantal Ianniciello, an immigration lawyer.
Plus généralement, les dossiers touchant: More generally, cases involving gender or sexuality are regularly very sensitive. The lawyer says she frequently has to defend people living with HIV.
« Il y a un refus total de parler de cel: “There is a total refusal to talk about it in front of the interpreter. Sometimes we have the interpreter step out and try to talk using simple words or with our hands. All the more so because their loved ones don’t know the person is living with it,” says the lawyer. If the claimant fears the interpreter will break professional confidentiality and reveal their story to their community, this discomfort can jeopardize their hearing and therefore their status. Indeed, since the commissioner has not been made aware of this issue, the discomfort can be misinterpreted, and crucial parts of the claimant’s story may be left out without the claimant being able to correct it.

On retrouve cette subjectivité chez tous: This subjectivity is found among all IRB commissioners. “We’re dealing with human beings, with the commissioners as much as with the claimants. Everyone has their baggage. Prejudices and judgments can be a big problem,” continues lawyer Chantal Ianniciello. She says there is sometimes difficulty understanding certain issues, especially when the asylum seeker’s story involves gender or sexual violence. At times, a story that doesn’t seem logical to the commissioner can look suspicious.
« Dans une demande d’asile, on juge l’au: “In an asylum claim, you’re judging the other person and you’re expected to remember what date you were beaten, how many times, how long it lasted. But what are those expectations based on? I’ve never been subjected to violence, and I tell myself I would remember, because it’s important,” explains Chantal Ianniciello. These same expectations came up during the hearing of a woman who had experienced an enormous amount of violence. “At first, it was a story of sexual assault.
Elle est tombée enceinte et ses parents: She got pregnant and her parents forced her to marry. She lived years of total hell with her abuser. Over all those years, she had 10 children and her husband cut off her fingers,” the lawyer says with emotion. While that last act seems the most serious, this woman did not see it as the worst thing in her own reality.
Étant en position d’autorité, les commis: Being in a position of authority, commissioners bear the heavy responsibility of deciding the future of people who have been settled in Quebec for several years. They must base their decisions on the story written by the claimant, the evidence provided and the answers given on the day of the hearing. However, that evidence can sometimes be hard to provide, which can cost a person their asylum. That is the case for an acquaintance of Linda’s, who was refused asylum because the commissioner did not believe he was really from Mauritania. “The board determined he was from Senegal and not Mauritania. They rejected his claim and both his appeals. All he has left is the humanitarian application,” she says.
« Ils doivent juger du bien-fondé d’une: “They have to judge the merits of a claim based on a feeling or their emotions. It’s random,” he says emphatically. Since every decision is discretionary, Frantz André finds it abnormal that no oversight exists to keep this practice in check. All the more so because IRB commissioners receive no specific training. “Anyone can be a commissioner. You just need to have held a management position. But when you’re not a lawyer and don’t know how to read legal documents, it can lead to errors,” he exclaims.
Pour les avocates Stéphanie Valois et Ch: For lawyers Stéphanie Valois and Chantal Ianniciello, commissioner training should be expanded. Their responsibility for another person’s life, as well as the need to question them on difficult subjects, even traumas, involves too much for their training to be neglected. “Understanding the other person’s point of view isn’t easy. They should be taught to better understand people so as to improve their judgment,” says Chantal Ianniciello, referring in particular to judgments about sexual violence.
En octobre dernier, <l1>la CISR annonçai: Last October, <l1>the IRB announced</l1> that it had set up a special team responsible for gender-based asylum claims (ESDAG). Twenty-four experts were brought together to think about these issues and were trained for four weeks. Their work began at the end of October. Like the issue of gender, the issue of race also seems to have been taken seriously by the IRB, following the recent Black Lives Matter movements.
Si bien qu’une réflexion est en cours po: So much so that a reflection is under way on what should be done to be more sensitive to the realities of minorities, to the other person’s point of view. An approach that is more than welcome, according to Chantal Ianniciello and Stéphanie Valois: “We’re white. How can we speak for Black people?” they ask. We asked the board to respond to these various initiatives, but we have not yet received an answer.
Pour les avocates, si ces réflexions ne: For the lawyers, while these reflections are not linked to the pandemic, the latter has certainly helped improve everyone’s tolerance: “everyone has seen what it’s like to live through major changes,” they say.
